title: Make a circuit dead and prove it
summary: Before you touch building wiring or an opened appliance: find every source of power, switch them all off, lock or tag them, and prove the circuit is dead with a meter you have just proved works. Never connect a generator to a building through a socket.

materials.item: Tape and a written note, or a padlock, to stop anyone switching back on
A known live source to prove the meter on: your own generator or inverter socket, or a battery on the DC range

steps.text: List every source that could feed the circuit: the grid, a generator, a solar inverter, a battery inverter, a UPS, or a second supply into the same building. Follow cables and look for panels, inverters and changeover switches.
steps.warn: Solar and battery systems can keep a building live with the grid dead.

steps.text: Switch off the main breaker or main switch. For solar, also switch off the inverter and its DC isolator. For a single appliance, unplug it and keep the plug where you can see it.
Tape or lock the switch in the off position and leave a note: Working on this. Do not switch on.
Put the black lead in COM and the red lead in V. Set the meter to AC volts on a range above the supply (600 V or higher, or auto). Prove the meter on a known live source.
steps.warn: With the red lead in an amps socket the meter is a dead short. Check the sockets before every voltage test.

steps.text: Test the circuit you'll work on: live to neutral, live to earth, and neutral to earth. All should read close to zero.
steps.warn: Hold the probes behind their finger guards and don't touch the metal tips. Keep your other hand away if you can.

steps.text: Prove the meter again on the known live source. If it doesn't read now, your test proved nothing: fix the meter and start again.
If the circuit has big capacitors (inverters, UPSes, motor drives, air conditioners), wait, discharge them with a resistor tool and measure.
Do your work. If you leave and come back, test again before touching anything.
When you're done, check that nobody is touching the circuit, put covers back, take off your lock or note, then switch on.

To run a building from a generator, use a proper changeover switch fitted by someone who knows how, or run extension leads from the generator straight to each appliance. Never plug a generator into a wall socket.
steps.warn: A double-ended plug lead can make the street wiring live and kill someone working on it, and its bare pins are live in your hand.

notes:
## Why live, dead, live

A meter with a flat battery, a blown fuse, a broken lead or the wrong setting reads zero on a live wire. Proving it on a known live source before and after your test is the only way to know your "zero" is real.

## Where power can come from after the grid goes down

| Source | How it gets into the wiring | What to switch off |
|---|---|---|
| Generator | Changeover switch, or a dangerous plug lead into a socket | Generator, and the changeover switch |
| Solar inverter | Connected to the panel or a sub-panel | Inverter AC switch and DC isolator; cover the panels |
| Battery inverter or large UPS | Hard-wired into a panel | Inverter, and its battery switch |
| Neighbour's system | Shared wiring in flats and terraces | Your main switch; test anyway |

## Voltages and colours

Mains is about 120 V in North America and parts of Latin America, and 220–240 V in most other places. Wire colours vary by country and age:

| Wiring | Live | Neutral | Earth |
|---|---|---|---|
| Europe and most newer installs | Brown | Blue | Green/yellow |
| Old UK | Red | Black | Green or bare |
| North America | Black or red | White | Green or bare |

Never trust colours. Old, DIY and repaired wiring breaks the rules. Test.

## Meter ratings

Meters are rated by category. CAT II is for sockets and appliances, CAT III for panels and fixed wiring. A cheap meter with no category and thin leads can explode in your hand on a panel fault. Use the best meter and leads you have.

## Common mistakes

- Switching off a light switch and assuming the fitting is dead. Some switches only break the neutral.
- Trusting a non-contact voltage pen alone. They miss things.
- Testing only live to neutral.
- Forgetting a second source.
- Leaving the red lead in the amps socket from the last job.
